To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) we discovered a live extreme scattering event (i.e., an event that was in progress) in the radio light curve of the radio source B0917+44; (2) this is only the second live event ever discovered; (3) we followed up the event with radio observations at 1.4, 4.8, and 8.4 GHz and optical observations at multiple wavelengths; (4) we modeled the radio data with a plasma lens model and found that

(i) a radio source in the constellation of Aquila was observed to brighten in real time; (ii) the source was identified as an ESE; (iii) follow-up radio and optical observations confirmed the identification of an ESE; and (iv) modeling of the radio data demonstrated that the lensing plasma is a density enhancement, ruling out one physical model for ESEs.

(1) a new technique was developed to identify ESEs in real time, (2) the first ESE was discovered with the new technique while it was in-progress, (3) the radio data from the ESE were analyzed and modeled, (4) the optical counterpart was observed and the lens was ruled out as a supernova remnant, and (5) the lensing structure was modeled and found to be a density enhancement.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the extreme scattering of radio signals from extragalactic radio sources, caused by the interstellar medium in our own Galaxy.

the study of extreme scattering events (E.SE.s), a class of astronomical phenomena that occur when radio waves from extragalactic radio sources are scattered by the interstellar plasma in the Milky Way Galaxy.
the study of radio waves that pass through the interstellar medium (ISM) of the Milky Way galaxy.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the ESE is a density enhancement with diverging geometry.
the lensing material is a density enhancement, and it is diverging, which rules out the model of the lensing material being a density enhancement, but converging.
the ESE lens is an isolated, diverging, high-density, and high-pressure cloud.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the ESEs are a result of a plasma lens in the Milky Way, which is a very rare event.
we have identified an ESE while the event is in progress, allowing us to follow up with radio and optical observations to constrain the physical model and the plasma properties.
we developed a new survey technique to find extreme scattering events, and we followed up on one of them.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we have demonstrated a technique for identifying live extreme scattering events (E.S.E.s), which are radio events that are caused by plasma lenses in the Milky Way's interstellar medium.
we have discovered a live extreme scattering event (or ESE).
ESEs can be detected in real time.
